items.bodyEn: Kusatsu, the 52nd post town, was the fork where the Nakasendō rejoined the Tōkaidō; from here the two highways ran as one to Kyoto. A stone signpost with a lantern top, raised in 1816, still points right for the Tōkaidō and Ise, left for the Nakasendō and Mino. The town's honjin survives, one of the largest on the road.
items.sourceNote: Kusatsu Oiwake stone signpost (1816); 草津宿本陣, national historic site

items.bodyEn: 急がば回れ, haste makes waste, was born here. Yabase in Kusatsu ran a ferry straight across Lake Biwa to Ōtsu, quick but exposed to sudden gales off Mount Hiei. A verse attributed to the renga poet Sōchō (1448–1532) advises the warrior to skip the boat and take the long way over the Seta bridge: 急がば回れ瀬田の長橋.
items.sourceNote: Seisuishō (醒睡笑, 1623): もののふの矢橋の船は速けれど急がば回れ瀬田の長橋, attributed to Sōchō

items.bodyEn: The かたい in 想像にかたくない is 難い, 'hard to do', a classical adjective that lives on in 信じがたい and 忘れがたい. Its most famous child is ありがたい: 有り難し meant 'hard to exist', hence rare, and from rare it drifted to precious and grateful. Say ありがとう and you are using the same word as this N1 pattern.
items.ja: {想像|そうぞう}に{難|かた}くない
items.kana: そうぞうにかたくない
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entries 難い(かたい), 有り難い: 「あることがむずかしい」→「めったにない」

items.bodyEn: Hiroshige titled his Kusatsu print 名物立場, 'famous rest stop', and drew not the post town but a roadside teahouse with a palanquin racing past. A 立場 was an informal halt between stations where bearers rested and travelers snacked. Kusatsu's specialty was 姥が餅: a bite of mochi wrapped in smooth red bean paste with a white dot on top.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō (c. 1833–34), 'Kusatsu: Famous Teahouse' (名物立場)
